overview: This 4-week intensive curriculum is designed to take a beginner from zero knowledge to a functional understanding of the modern data analyst toolkit. Learners will progress through the data analysis lifecycle, mastering Excel for data manipulation, SQL for database querying, Data Visualization principles for communication, and a basic introduction to Python for automated analysis.
learning_objectives: Understand the six stages of the data analysis life cycle: Ask, Prepare, Process, Analyze, Share, and Act.
Master advanced spreadsheet functions (VLOOKUP, Pivot Tables) for data cleaning and initial analysis.
Write SQL queries to extract, filter, and aggregate data from relational databases.
Apply data visualization best practices to create compelling charts and dashboards.
Comprehend the basics of Python programming and the Pandas library for data handling.

topics.title: The Data Analysis Process
topics.description: A comprehensive walkthrough of the six stages of the analytics life cycle - Ask, Prepare, Process, Analyze, Share, and Act - and how each stage builds on the previous one. You will learn how a clear business question shapes the data you collect, why preparation and cleaning often consume the bulk of an analyst's time, and how processing decisions ripple downstream into the analysis itself. By the end of this topic you should be able to explain each phase in your own words, identify which phase a real-world task belongs to, and describe what artifacts (questions, cleaned datasets, dashboards, recommendations) flow between phases. This framework becomes the backbone for every other lesson in the course.

topics.title: What is Data Analysis?
topics.description: A grounded look at what data analysts actually do day-to-day, including the difference between data analysis and data science, the kinds of questions analysts answer, and the tools they typically reach for. We contrast descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, and prescriptive analytics so you can recognize each style in the wild, and we walk through several short case studies - a marketing funnel review, an operations bottleneck investigation, and a product retention deep-dive - to show how analysts translate vague stakeholder asks into concrete data questions. You will leave with a clear mental model of the analyst role and the kinds of problems where this skill set creates value.

topics.title: Excel Formulas and Functions
topics.description: A hands-on tour of the Excel formulas that show up in nearly every analyst's workflow: IF and IFS for conditional logic, VLOOKUP and XLOOKUP for joining tables across sheets, and the small ecosystem of text and date helpers that turn raw exports into useful columns. You will learn how to compose these functions, debug common errors like #N/A and #REF, and structure formulas so that they remain readable as a workbook grows. We also cover absolute vs. relative references, named ranges, and a few patterns (lookup-with-fallback, layered IFS, error-tolerant matches) that scale from quick spreadsheets to shared team workbooks.

topics.title: Data Cleaning in Excel
topics.description: Practical techniques for taking a messy spreadsheet and turning it into something an analyst can actually trust. You will practice removing duplicates with awareness of which columns define uniqueness, splitting concatenated fields with Text-to-Columns and Flash Fill, normalizing inconsistent text with TRIM, CLEAN, and PROPER, and handling missing values without silently dropping rows. We close with a guided exercise that uses conditional formatting to spot anomalies - outliers, unexpected blanks, and duplicate keys - before they corrupt downstream analysis. The goal is to build a repeatable cleaning checklist you can run before any analysis.

topics.title: Pivot Tables in Excel
topics.description: A deep dive into Pivot Tables - arguably the highest-leverage feature in Excel for an analyst. You will learn how a Pivot Table reshapes a flat dataset into rows, columns, and aggregated values; how to swap dimensions on the fly to test different views; and how slicers and timelines turn a static table into an interactive mini-dashboard. We cover calculated fields for ratios and per-row metrics that the source data does not provide, Pivot Charts for quickly visualizing aggregations, and best practices around source data structure (one row per observation, no merged cells) that make Pivot Tables behave predictably as the data grows.

topics.title: Introduction to Relational Databases
topics.description: An accessible introduction to relational database management systems (RDBMS) - what they are, why companies store their operational data in them, and how that shapes the data an analyst sees. You will learn how tables, rows, and columns map to real-world entities, why primary keys uniquely identify a row and why foreign keys define relationships across tables, and how normalization keeps data consistent at the cost of more joins later. We then walk through the anatomy of a basic SELECT statement (SELECT, FROM, DISTINCT, ORDER BY) so the syntax we layer on next week sits on a solid foundation rather than feeling like memorized incantations.

topics.title: SQL Aggregate Functions
topics.description: A thorough look at how to summarize and slice data inside the database using SQL. You will practice writing WHERE clauses with comparison, BETWEEN, IN, and pattern-matching operators to filter rows precisely, then layer aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX) on top to compute group-level metrics. We dedicate special attention to GROUP BY (and the common bug where SELECT columns do not match the grouping) and to HAVING - the filter that runs after aggregation, on the aggregated values themselves. The lesson ends with a short library of aggregation patterns (top-N per group, distinct counts, conditional sums) that you will reach for again and again.

topics.title: Visualizing SQL Joins
topics.description: A visual, intuition-first explanation of how SQL joins combine rows from multiple tables. You will see how INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, and FULL OUTER joins map to overlapping circles in a Venn diagram and, more importantly, what each join does to the row count of your result set when keys are missing on one side. We also cover the common pitfalls - accidental row explosions when join keys are not unique, NULL behavior in outer joins, and the difference between a UNION and a JOIN - so you can predict the shape of a query's output before you run it.

topics.title: SQL Joins Practice
topics.description: Hands-on practice combining multiple tables to answer realistic business questions. You will write queries that enrich a transactions table with customer attributes, compute per-segment summaries that span three or more tables, and use UNION (and UNION ALL) to stitch together datasets with the same schema. Along the way we discuss when to push aggregation before vs. after a join, how to debug joins that produce duplicates, and how aliasing tables and columns keeps multi-join queries readable. The goal is to leave this lesson comfortable joining several tables in a single query without losing track of what each row represents.

topics.title: Data Visualization Fundamentals
topics.description: An introduction to the design principles that separate a chart that informs from one that misleads. You will study the role of preattentive attributes (position, length, color, shape) and how each one maps to the kinds of comparisons readers can make at a glance. We discuss the data-ink ratio and decluttering - removing chart junk so the data carries the message - and how to manage cognitive load by choosing a small number of strong visual encodings rather than many weak ones. The lesson closes with a critique of three real charts, identifying what works, what misleads, and how each could be redesigned for clarity.

topics.title: Choosing the Right Chart
topics.description: A practical guide to picking a chart type that matches both the data you have and the question your audience is asking. You will learn when to reach for a bar chart vs. a line chart, why pie charts often fail, and the trade-offs between scatter plots, heatmaps, and small multiples for showing relationships across many groups. We walk through a decision flow - starting from the comparison you want the reader to make (across categories, over time, between distributions, between parts and a whole) - that you can apply when designing your own visualizations. By the end you should be able to defend each chart choice in a dashboard with a one-sentence rationale.

topics.title: Tableau for Beginners
topics.description: A guided walkthrough of getting productive in Tableau Public, starting from connecting to a CSV or spreadsheet through to building your first analytical worksheet. You will learn how Tableau classifies fields as dimensions vs. measures, why that distinction drives every drag-and-drop visualization you build, and how marks, shelves, and the show-me menu work together to suggest chart types. We cover continuous vs. discrete fields, basic calculated fields, and the workflow of iterating between a worksheet and your underlying data to spot quality issues. By the end you'll have a small portfolio of single-view charts you've built yourself.

topics.title: Building Dashboards in Tableau
topics.description: An end-to-end lesson on combining multiple worksheets into a coherent, interactive dashboard. You will learn how Tableau's tiled vs. floating layouts behave at different screen sizes, how to use containers to keep alignment under control, and how filters, parameters, and dashboard actions let a viewer drill from a high-level overview into specific subsets. We also cover information hierarchy - title, KPIs, supporting charts, drill-down - and the principle of designing for the question your audience will ask first. You'll finish by publishing a small dashboard to Tableau Public and sharing the link.

modules.module_title: Week 4: Introduction to Python for Data

topics.title: Python Programming Fundamentals
topics.description: A from-scratch introduction to Python aimed at analysts coming from Excel and SQL. You will learn how variables, core data types (int, float, str, bool), and control flow (if/else, for, while) compose into small scripts, and how lists and dictionaries become the everyday containers for tabular and key-value data. We also introduce functions for reusing logic, basic error handling so a single bad row does not crash an entire script, and the Jupyter Notebook environment - cells, kernels, and the iterative workflow that makes notebooks ideal for analysis. The lesson ends with a short exercise that translates a familiar Excel transformation into a Python equivalent.

topics.title: Getting Started with Pandas
topics.description: An introduction to the two core Pandas data structures - Series (a labeled 1-D array) and DataFrame (a labeled 2-D table) - and how they let you express analysis in a few lines of expressive code. You will learn how to read CSV and Excel files into a DataFrame, inspect it with head, info, and describe, and select rows and columns using both label-based (.loc) and position-based (.iloc) indexing. We discuss why Pandas operations return new objects rather than mutating in place, how chained assignments cause subtle bugs, and the small handful of patterns (assign, query, pipe) that keep analytical code readable as it grows.

topics.title: Data Analysis with Python and Pandas
topics.description: A hands-on lesson that takes a real dataset from raw CSV to a finished mini-analysis. You will practice filtering rows, creating derived columns, grouping with groupby and aggregating with multiple functions, and merging DataFrames with the same mental model you built for SQL joins. Along the way we cover descriptive statistics (mean, median, std, percentiles), spotting outliers, and the basic plotting hooks that Pandas exposes through Matplotlib. The lesson ends with a guided write-up: turning the numbers you computed into a short narrative - finding, evidence, and recommendation - the way you would present them to a stakeholder.

topics.title: Data Analysis Capstone Project
topics.description: A capstone project that ties together every skill in the course: pick a public dataset that interests you, formulate two or three sharp analytical questions, and run a full analysis using whichever combination of Excel, SQL, Tableau, and Python feels right for each step. You will document your process in a notebook or report - what you asked, what you cleaned, what you found, what you would do next - and present your findings as if to a non-technical stakeholder. The deliverable is intentionally open-ended so you practice the judgment calls real analysts make: scoping the question, choosing the right tools, and structuring a story around the evidence rather than a dump of charts.
